[Thinking]
**Creating a study plan**

I want to provide a structured study plan that includes techniques like spaced repetition, active recall, and the Pomodoro method. I'll address the user's study environment, prioritization, and exam types while also touching on practice papers, memory techniques, stress management, sleep, nutrition, and day-of-exam tips. 

I should ask clarifying questions to tailor the plan. It will be concise yet actionable, with steps and options. I'll include a sample weekly plan and daily routine based on evidence-based methods. What subject or exam are we focusing on, and what's the timeframe?
[/Thinking]

Here’s a simple, effective way to prepare, based on what works best for most students. If you share your exam dates, subjects, and current standing, I can tailor this.

1) Set targets and schedule
- List all topics per subject; mark them as A (weak), B (okay), C (strong).
- Plan backward from exam dates. Aim for 2–3 focused study blocks per day per subject in rotation.
- Use a weekly template:
  - Mon–Fri: 2–4 Pomodoros (25 min study + 5 min break) per subject; evenings for review/questions.
  - Sat: Full practice sets or past papers.
  - Sun: Light review + planning.

2) Use high-yield methods
- Active recall: Close notes and try to answer from memory; write or say answers.
- Spaced repetition: Revisit topics 1 day, 3 days, 7 days later. Use flashcards (Anki/Quizlet) for facts.
- Practice questions: Do past exams under timed conditions; review every mistake and make a “weakness list.”
- Interleaving: Mix similar topics (e.g., calculus + physics problems) to improve transfer.
- Note compression: Turn notes into one-page “cheat sheets” per topic.

3) Per subject approach
- Problem-heavy (math, physics, CS): 70–80% time on problems. Start with worked examples, then untimed sets, then timed mixed sets. Keep an error log: problem, why missed, fix.
- Content-heavy (bio, history): 30% read/organize, 70% recall (flashcards, blurting, teaching aloud). Use diagrams and timelines.
- Essay-based: Build outlines, thesis statements, and evidence banks. Practice timed outlines and 1–2 full essays weekly with feedback.
- Languages: Daily small doses—vocab SRS, short writing, reading, and speaking/listening drills.

4) Daily routine (example)
- Block 1: New learning on priority topic (Pomodoro x2).
- Short break + quick walk.
- Block 2: Practice questions or past paper sections (Pomodoro x2).
- Lunch + 20–30 min light review (flashcards).
- Block 3: Review mistakes and redo missed problems (Pomodoro x1–2).
- Evening: 15–20 min spaced review; set tomorrow’s goals.

5) Exam week
- Shift to 60–70% practice papers and recall, 30–40% review.
- Do at least two full timed past papers per subject if possible.
- Two days before: Only light new material; focus on weaknesses and summary sheets.
- Day before: Brief review, pack materials, sleep 7–9 hours.
- Day of: Quick recall drills only; no cramming.

6) Productivity and wellbeing
- Remove friction: tidy desk, website blockers, phone out of room.
- Energy: sleep 7–9h, hydrate, protein + complex carbs, short exercise breaks.
- Motivation: Start with a 5-minute timer; track streaks; reward finished blocks.

7) Tools
- Anki/Quizlet for spaced repetition.
- Notion/Google Sheets for plan + tracking.
- Forest/Focus To-Do for Pomodoro.
- Past papers from your exam board’s site.

If you tell me:
- Subjects and exam formats
- Dates/time left
- Your current strengths/weaknesses
I’ll build a customized week-by-week plan and a daily schedule.
